Incident: Binance $6.3 billion cryptocurrency theft
Victims / Targets: Binance (cryptocurrency exchange); ~$6.34B stolen, ~$2.85B frozen (Binance)
Actors (as reported): TraderTraitor (FBI and US Secret Service: North Korea's TraderTraitor (North Korea denied involvement))
Summary: FBI and USSS attributed the theft to North Korea's TraderTraitor and urged exchanges and DeFi operators to block transactions with or derived from its addresses; stolen funds were converted mainly to Ethereum. Binance's post-mortem describes a months-long campaign from June 2026: a fake job interview with a malicious coding assignment and "AI coding tool" installer compromised an employee device (~September), the attacker evaded EDR, moved laterally from 20 Oct, reached wallet tooling by 29 Oct and used compromised credentials to authorize transactions. Elliptic traced ~12,000 wallets across 11 blockchains. Elliptic (tracker updated 26 Nov): $6.43B stolen on 29 Oct across 11 blockchains, $2.85B frozen or seized, stablecoins 54% ($3.46B); funds "very likely still held by North Korea". Since 17 Nov ~488,000 ETH has left the main holdings, ~125,000 ETH swapped for ~3,470 BTC and at least 6,330 BTC ($389M) sent into coinjoins (mostly Kruw); ~$16M went to addresses holding proceeds of the September 2026 Bitget exploit, "also believed to be the work of TraderTraitor". Elliptic's blocklist covers more than 33,000 addresses. SecurityWeek: the FBI alert lists 628 addresses (608 Ethereum, 19 Bitcoin, 1 Solana).
Reporters: FBI; The Record; The Record; Elliptic; SecurityWeek
Keywords: Binance; TraderTraitor; Kruw; Bitget
Notes: The FBI alert lists 628 wallet addresses and Elliptic publishes a 33,000+ address blocklist (https://www.elliptic.co/binance-hack-2026-blocklist/); neither was read, so no addresses are recorded here. Elliptic's page has inconsistent ETH and wallet-count figures; the SecurityWeek date is approximate (page undated). Theft-date details come from Binance's post-mortem as reported by The Record.

Victims / Targets: 1Password (password manager); "only a small number of users were affected" (1Password via BleepingComputer), notified individually. Customer vaults and their encryption keys not compromised (1Password).

Incident: ARTEX agentic AI penetration-testing framework abused in intrusions
Victims / Targets: Hundreds of organizations; South Korean banks (loan-inquiry and employee mobile systems); IT and software vendors and their downstream Microsoft 365 tenants via ConnectWise multi-tenant app credentials; exposed web APIs and identity providers
Sectors: Financial services; Cryptocurrency; Government; Telecommunications; Defense; Aerospace; Semiconductors; Technology; Software; Pharmaceuticals
Actors (as reported): Storm-0940 (Microsoft: China-state aligned actor); Vapor Panda (CrowdStrike (via Talos): China-nexus espionage campaign from 17 Oct 2026); Salt Typhoon (Microsoft (via The Record, 2026-11-25): Chinese state-backed group that has integrated Artex); Crystal Typhoon (Microsoft (via The Record, 2026-11-25): Chinese state-backed group that has integrated Artex); Storm-3358 (Talos: financially motivated, Cambodia-based, targets financial organizations in Southeast Asia); Unnamed Chinese-speaking actor (CrowdStrike: likely Chinese-speaking and financially motivated (moderate confidence))
Summary: ARTEX, an open-source autonomous multi-agent AI penetration-testing framework published in July 2026 (closed-sourced on 8 Oct after 12,000+ forks), has been used by several unrelated actors; Talos says it is largely used by financially motivated criminals and China-nexus actors, so ARTEX use alone does not identify an actor. An LLM planner drives worker agents running nmap, nuclei, httpx, ffuf and curl. CrowdStrike: an unnamed, likely Chinese-speaking, financially motivated actor breached South Korean bank systems and exfiltrated data (late Sep to early Oct). Microsoft: China-state aligned Storm-0940 password-sprayed 2,250+ tenants (10-14 Oct) and abused ConnectWise multi-tenant application credentials for a supply-chain compromise, in some cases gaining privileged cloud access in under 3 hours; Wiz saw the same actor expand to other IT and software vendors. Unit 42: intrusion attempts (24 Sep-27 Oct) harvested JS source maps and OpenAPI specs, probed OAuth flows, self-registered accounts and read ~50 MB of API data; infrastructure serves WWW-Authenticate Basic realm="ARTEX" and a Sub2API LLM gateway. FBI FLASH-20261113-001 (TLP:CLEAR) gives network and behavioral IOCs, names no state sponsor, and lists Storm-3358 WISP C2 nodes and ARTEX servers (Microsoft). SentinelOne ties VAPOR PANDA's ARTEX use to BLOODALCHEMY malware. Separately, BadByte found trojanized ARTEX Docker images (tomicdd/artex, congdonglinux/artex; 7,946 pulls) whose /app/artex binary runs the login request's captcha field via sh -c as root before authentication, i.e. anyone running that image was exposed; Docker removed both images on 5 Nov 2026. On 25 Nov Microsoft (via The Record) said Chinese state-backed Crystal Typhoon and Salt Typhoon have integrated Artex for "network reconnaissance, credential attacks, and web application exploitation", that unnamed North Korean groups also use it, and that it "does not introduce new attack techniques".
Reporters: Microsoft Threat Intelligence; The Record (Microsoft); Cisco Talos; Microsoft Threat Intelligence; CrowdStrike; Wiz; Palo Alto Networks Unit 42; FBI (FLASH-20261113-001); SentinelOne; BadByte; Kodem Security
Keywords: ARTEX; Sub2API; lanmao666; BLOODALCHEMY; Storm-0940; Storm-3358; Vapor Panda; tomicdd; Salt Typhoon; Crystal Typhoon
Notes: Talos and Unit 42 note that not all ARTEX activity is malicious (it is also used for authorized testing), so these IPs are indicators to investigate rather than block outright. Generic user agents (curl, python-requests, Python-urllib) are omitted. SentinelOne's appendix also lists SHA-256 hashes for VAPOR PANDA's GameHook binary and BLOODALCHEMY loader/payload, an ARTEX TLS certificate hash and Hunt.io-sourced IPs; they were not added because the page could not be read verbatim past mid-appendix.
IOC Types: sha256 1, ipv4 2582, domain 6, user-agent 6, http-header 1, docker-image 3, app-id 3, other 2

Incident: Hex.pm package registry servers compromised via CVSS 10.0 RCE (CVE-2026-129514)
Activity Period: 2026-11-23 (exploit requests 18:16-18:29 UTC; related activity from the same addresses since the prior week)
Victims / Targets: Hex.pm, the Elixir/Erlang package registry: OS commands run on six production web servers. Database contents (email addresses, password hashes, 2FA secrets, session data, possibly private packages) could not be ruled out as read; the team says no package was changed.
Summary: Per The Hacker News, summarising the Hex.pm team's incident report: an attacker exploited CVE-2026-129514 (CVSS 10.0), an unauthenticated request-body parsing flaw present since February 2016 that accepted maps with a __struct__ key, to run OS commands on six Hex.pm production servers on Monday 23 Nov. Load balancer logs show 69 exploit requests between 18:16 and 18:29 UTC from two addresses; all servers were on a patched build within about 15 minutes of the first malicious request. Earlier activity from the same addresses "suggests the attacker built a local copy of hex.pm to test against". Hex.pm logged out all users and rotated session/token keys; the registry signing key had not yet been rotated. Reported to Sweden's data protection authority, CISA and ENISA. "Who was behind the attack is unknown." Related library CVEs: CVE-2026-124283 (ash), CVE-2026-133555 (db_connection), CVE-2026-130411 (flop).
Reporters: Hex.pm (primary incident report; not read - fetch blocked); Hex.pm GitHub advisory (not read - fetch blocked); The Hacker News
Keywords: Hex.pm; hexpm; Elixir; Erlang; CVE-2026-129514; GHSA-9pmm-hf4r-27pg

Incident: GT13 intrusion campaign against Check Point Security Management servers (24 servers, 22 organizations)
Activity Period: 2026-10-02 to 2026-11-02 (GreyNoise expects the campaign is ongoing)
Victims / Targets: GreyNoise: 24 Check Point Security Management servers compromised across at least 22 organizations; victim assets in the UK, Ireland, France, Netherlands, Greece, Germany, Austria, Bulgaria, Poland, India, Thailand, Vietnam, South Korea, Hong Kong, China, Australia and the US. SecurityWeek lists energy, engineering, financial services, government, manufacturing, mining and transportation. Targeting "does not appear to be focused on any specific geography or industry sector" (GreyNoise).
Sectors: Energy; Engineering; Financial Services; Government; Manufacturing; Mining; Transportation
Countries: United Kingdom; Ireland; France; Netherlands; Greece; Germany; Austria; Bulgaria; Poland; India; Thailand; Vietnam; South Korea; Hong Kong; China; Australia; United States
Actors (as reported): GT13 (GreyNoise: 'We do not attribute GT13 to any known or publicly tracked threat group at this time. We do not currently have enough information to make assessments relating to the motivation of the actor or alignment to a nation-of-origin.')
Summary: GreyNoise ("99 IPs but a C2 ain't one", 23 Nov 2026): an actor it tracks as GreyNoise Threat 13 (GT13) gained access to a Rejetto HFS server via CVE-2026-61500 (forging an admin session cookie after recovering the signing key) and used it as a hop for exfiltration and for access to Check Point Security Management servers, where CVE-2026-16232 (SmartConsole auth bypass to Run Script) was used to run commands. Data from 24 management servers was collected on the hop, including firewall databases, Internal CA files, credentials, firewall configuration and a newly minted certificate (pivot.p12); the actor also attempted to unload security policies. Tooling: Nmap, Chisel, Impacket, Paramiko and 30+ Python scripts; persistence via /etc/ld.so.preload (/usr/lib/.libproc.so) and appended SSH keys; a "ZULT" implant downloaded from data-zt.newpayapp.com. GreyNoise also describes probing of other edge and internal services (Citrix NetScaler, Ivanti, Exchange, VMware vCenter, NetLogon, Oracle TNS). Traffic came from ExpressVPN egress IPs or compromised victim devices. GreyNoise believes the actor used "LLMs and agentic systems" for scanning, exploitation, tool development and automated interaction, alongside hands-on-keyboard activity.
Reporters: GreyNoise; SecurityWeek
Keywords: GT13; Check Point; Security Management; SmartConsole; CVE-2026-16232; CVE-2026-61500; Rejetto; HFS; ZULT; newpayapp
Notes: Not captured: the ~69 IP rows in GreyNoise's Indicators table (all tagged AS206092 ExpressVPN egress, each with its own activity window); shared commercial-VPN addresses with high false-positive risk and the table was read in two passes, so take them from the GreyNoise page directly. Incident: Microsoft Agent Framework PyPI package compromised with a cloud-credential stealer
Victims / Targets: Users and CI pipelines that installed agent-framework 1.26.1 or 1.26.2 from PyPI during the exposure window; the package has about 190,000 downloads a month (Aikido). Wiz saw 50 requests captured by the webhook.site endpoint, 17 of them representing three unique, successful cases of victim-data exfiltration
Summary: Two malicious releases of Microsoft's official agent-framework Python package (1.26.1 and 1.26.2) were published to PyPI 33 minutes apart on 17 Nov 2026 and quarantined (StepSecurity: 1.26.1 at 21:06:16 UTC, 1.26.2 at 21:16:44 UTC). Each added a .pth start-up hook (agent_framework_meta.pth in 1.26.1, af_runtime_diag.pth in 1.26.2) that runs the stealer on every Python start without importing the package. It harvests environment variables, /proc/*/environ, Azure CLI files, .npmrc, pip.conf, .netrc, .git-credentials and Docker config, tries to mint Azure DevOps OIDC, Azure managed-identity and (1.26.2) GitHub Actions OIDC tokens, and POSTs zlib-compressed, Base64-encoded data to a webhook.site URL. Aikido: the releases were uploaded "with valid publishing credentials"; Wiz: the attacker "appears to have compromised a client certificate and private key for Microsoft ESRP" (a first publish attempt from AWS was rejected by ESRP IP filtering, a second from Microsoft-owned IP space succeeded); how the credentials were obtained is not known. Wiz says the tooling identifies itself as Cairn, an open-source AI penetration-testing framework, and has not linked the incident to the earlier durabletask compromise. Microsoft made some repositories private (including microsoft/agent-framework and microsoft/onnxruntime) "while we investigate malicious content". 1.26.0 is the last clean release; anyone who installed 1.26.1/1.26.2 should remove them and rotate exposed credentials. No actor named.
Reporters: Socket; Aikido Security; Wiz; StepSecurity; OX Security; Endor Labs; The Hacker News
Keywords: agent-framework; agent_framework_meta.pth; af_runtime_diag.pth; af_runtime_diag.py; _AF_TEL; runtime-diagnostics/1; af-runtime-diagnostics/1; ESRP; Cairn

Incident: Operation Snowball - jailbroken AI agent intrusion at a European telecom via Cisco BroadWorks (CVE-2026-20320)
Activity Period: 2026 (more than two weeks; dates not reported)
Victims / Targets: An unnamed European telecommunications provider and 13 organizations hosted on its data centre and cloud infrastructure (unclear whether all 13 were breached), including a healthcare organization; ~80 Zabbix monitoring backups covering the provider's managed-services customers. Claimed (from the agent's own reports, not confirmed with victims): dozens of credential sets and private keys, the healthcare organization's Active Directory data, subscriber billing records and "millions of patient records" from a TrakCare Oracle database with default credentials.
Actors (as reported): Unnamed Chinese-speaking operator (Operation Snowball) (Malbear Labs: activity consistent with a Chinese-origin operator; not linked to a state actor (Infosecurity Magazine paraphrase))
Summary: Malbear Labs (8 Nov 2026) found an attacker's exposed working directory with 70+ session transcripts and reports of a custom agent framework running a jailbroken DeepSeek Flash model (~78,000-character jailbreak prompt), which the operator "delegated the intrusion to ... and checked in asynchronously to review progress". Per Malbear: "The agent exploited CVE-2026-20320, an unauthenticated XXE in the BroadWorks OCI XML parser", recovering a system identity private key and SSL credential sets from the XSP host; the BroadWorks Provisioning Server was also exposed via an unauthenticated directory listing. It then got root on a Liferay host spanning several internal networks (CVE-2020-7961), a second foothold via JBoss/RichFaces (CVE-2013-2165), had a PwnKit (CVE-2021-4034) attempt blocked by endpoint security, and wrote its own replacement when a tunnelling tool was blocked. CISA added CVE-2026-20320 to KEV on 10 Nov 2026 (FCEB due 24 Nov); Cisco patched it in August.

Incident: Destructive wiper attack on Russian hosting provider Beget's cloud platform
Victims / Targets: Beget (Russian hosting provider and second-largest .RU registrar); VPS, S3 and Kubernetes data wiped; more than 200,000 customers, hundreds of websites disrupted
Summary: On the night of 1 Nov 2026 an attacker "gained access to the management layer of its entire architecture and then executed data-zeroing scripts" (BleepingComputer, citing Beget), wiping all cloud-infrastructure data: VPS, S3 and Kubernetes, plus CDN settings and IP configurations. VPS binary backups were "completely lost"; file backups survived for about half of VPS users, and Beget said "it is impossible to recover all data". The Record: the attack "disrupted hundreds of websites", including the Naryan-Mar city administration site and Chestny Znak; Beget has not disclosed initial access and found no evidence customer data was downloaded or modified, and urged customers to change passwords and access keys. About 1,000 servers needed manual inspection; by ~9 Nov 60% of shared hosting and 40% of dedicated servers were restored. Beget was sanctioned by the EU earlier in 2026. "No hacking group has publicly claimed responsibility for the incident" (The Record).
